title: Prayer, Wise Speech, and Friends in the Gospel
summary: Paul finishes the household instructions by telling masters to treat their slaves justly, remembering their own Master in heaven. He asks the church to devote itself to prayer, to pray that he may proclaim the mystery of Christ clearly, and to speak graciously and wisely to outsiders. He then introduces the letter carriers, Tychicus and Onesimus, sends greetings from his fellow workers, asks that the letter be shared with Laodicea, and signs off in his own hand.
story: The letter began with Christ's supremacy over all creation and ends with a list of names. That is not a letdown but the point: the Lord of the universe is served in particular friendships, travels, and tasks. The final verses of the household code (verse 1) close the discussion of chapter 3, and the calls to prayer and wise speech turn the church outward toward the unbelievers around them. The greetings show the network of coworkers who carried the gospel across the Roman world, and several names link this letter to Philemon, Acts, and Paul's later letters, letting us glimpse how the early church actually worked.
historical:
Paul was in chains (verses 3 and 18), awaiting trial. Tychicus, from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4), was one of his trusted messengers; he also carried Ephesians (Ephesians 6:21) and is mentioned later in 2 Timothy 4:12 and Titus 3:12. With him traveled Onesimus, a slave who had left his master Philemon and come to Paul, become a believer, and was now being sent back, as the letter to Philemon explains (whether he had run away, as most have thought, or had sought Paul out to plead for him in a dispute is debated). That Colossians calls him one of you strongly suggests that Philemon's household was in Colossae.

Several other names are familiar. Aristarchus of Thessalonica had been with Paul in the riot at Ephesus and on the voyage to Rome (Acts 19:29; 27:2). Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, was the John Mark who had left Paul and Barnabas partway through their first missionary trip, leading to a sharp disagreement between them (Acts 13:13; 15:37-39); here he is restored and commended, and in 2 Timothy 4:11 Paul calls him useful. Luke is named only here as a physician, and because Paul lists him apart from the Jewish coworkers of verses 10 and 11, most conclude he was a Gentile; tradition credits him with the Gospel of Luke and Acts. Demas would later desert Paul (2 Timothy 4:10). Laodicea and Hierapolis were nearby cities in the Lycus valley, and the letter from Laodicea (verse 16) has not survived. Some suggest it was the letter we call Ephesians, which may have circulated among several churches; others think it was a separate letter now lost. A short Latin Epistle to the Laodiceans that circulated in the Middle Ages is generally regarded as a later composition.
cultural:
Letters in the Roman world were carried by trusted travelers, since there was no public postal service for private people. The letter carrier often added news in person and sometimes explained or read the letter, which is why Paul says Tychicus will tell you all the news about me. Paul usually dictated his letters to a secretary (compare Romans 16:22) and added a closing greeting in his own hand, as a mark of authenticity and a personal touch; here the chained hand writing the greeting gives weight to the words remember my chains.

Churches met in homes. Nympha hosted the church in her house (verse 15); some later manuscripts read a male name, Nymphas, and the church in his house, but the feminine form is well supported and widely accepted. Wealthier believers who had larger houses often served as hosts and patrons. Letters were read aloud to the gathered church and then passed between congregations, which is part of how Paul's letters came to be collected. The phrase seasoned with salt (verse 6) described speech that was witty, pleasing, and well chosen; salt also preserved food and gave it flavor.
literary: The chapter is the letter's closing section. Verse 1 completes the household code begun in 3:18. Verses 2 to 6 give final general instructions in two pairs: prayer, including prayer for Paul's mission (verses 2 to 4), and conduct and speech toward outsiders (verses 5 and 6). Verses 7 to 9 commend the letter carriers. Verses 10 to 14 pass on greetings from six coworkers, three Jewish (Aristarchus, Mark, and Jesus called Justus) and three Gentile (Epaphras, Luke, and Demas). Verses 15 to 17 give instructions: greet the Laodiceans and Nympha, exchange letters, and pass on a charge to Archippus. Verse 18 is Paul's signature and blessing. Many of these features match the closing of Philemon, and the list of names is one of the strongest arguments for the letter's close connection to Paul's own circle.

outline.t: Wisdom and gracious speech toward outsiders
Greetings to Laodicea, and a word for Archippus
Paul's greeting in his own hand

doctrines.note: Paul calls the church to be devoted to prayer, watchful and thankful (verse 2), and he describes Epaphras as always wrestling in prayer for them (verse 12). Prayer is work, and it is shared: Paul, in chains, asks for prayer that God will open a door for the word.

Paul asks for an open door and for clarity in proclaiming the mystery of Christ, even in prison. Ordinary believers share the mission through wise conduct and gracious speech toward outsiders, ready to answer everyone (verses 5 and 6).

The chapter shows the church as a network of named people: coworkers, hosts, messengers, a returning slave, and churches sharing letters. Its unity crosses lines of ethnicity and social class, with Jews and Gentiles, a slave and householders, all named as brothers and fellow workers.

words.note: Exagorazo, to buy up or redeem. The word comes from the marketplace (agora) and means to buy something out or make the most of it. Redeeming the time means seizing each opportunity, especially in dealings with outsiders, as a merchant snaps up a bargain. The word for time here, kairos, means an opportune moment rather than time in general.

Thura, door. Paul uses an open door as a picture of opportunity for the gospel (compare 1 Corinthians 16:9 and 2 Corinthians 2:12). Here he is literally behind a locked door in chains, yet he asks not for release but for an open door for the word.

Desmos, bond or chain. Paul was physically bound, perhaps chained to a guard. His closing request, remember my chains, asks the church to pray for him and to remember that the gospel they received cost its messengers dearly.

christ: Even masters have a Master in heaven (verse 1), so the lordship of Christ, which chapter 1 set over all creation, reaches into the relationship where earthly power was most absolute. Paul's chains are for the mystery of Christ (verse 3), the long-hidden plan now revealed that God welcomes the Gentiles into his people through Christ. His coworkers labor for the kingdom of God (verse 11), and Epaphras is a servant of Christ Jesus (verse 12). The mention of Onesimus returning as a faithful and beloved brother is itself a small picture of what Christ does: a slave who had left his master comes back as family. The letter closes with grace, the free gift of God in Christ that the whole letter has proclaimed.
questions: Paul asks for an open door for the word while he is in chains. How might you pray for opportunities rather than only for relief in a hard situation?
What would it look like for your speech to be always gracious and seasoned with salt, especially with people who do not share your faith?
Mark had once failed Paul and is now commended. What does his story say about how the church should treat those who have fallen short?
